concerns.rationale: Additional verification controls form part of the device-binding standard across units 196–200. They do not identify or establish performance of second.duty; the exception and edition uncertainty remain.
Confirmation that the device belongs to the legitimate client precedes registration. This prerequisite remains unrepresented by the original questions.
This fragment completes the registration purpose and connects to the following guidance duty. It cannot independently establish second.duty.
Clear guidance for clients who lose a bound device is a distinct duty. Its performance is not captured by a gift-prohibition result.
Guidance must address deregistration and replacement binding. Both components remain outside the original formalization.
This continuation introduces examples of replacement-device guidance, not an independent universal procedure. The synthetic concern remains unresolved.
The example places deregistration of the lost device first. Its sequence and alternative procedures must remain visible; no performance facts are supplied.
Contacting the hotline is one example route, completed by identity verification in the next unit. It is not the only permitted route.
The text preserves a hotline route with identity verification and an alternative self-service route. Neither is represented by second.duty.
Self-service deregistration depends on the client being able to log in. The qualifying authentication alternatives continue in unit 208.
Another previously bound device or other authentication methods may support the example's login prerequisite. This alternative must not be reduced to a bound-device-only rule.
The replacement-binding example follows deregistration of the lost device. This sequencing condition does not resolve the unidentified second duty.
Replacement binding uses robust verification methods. Robustness requires assessment and cannot be inferred from a method label or the original questions.
The post-implementation-period restriction must be read with unit 212, the main timeline, and the existing-device exception. It does not require all existing devices to be rebound.
Robust verification is required for binding after the period; the following methods are examples. Neither their enumeration nor the timing alone establishes compliance.
This fragment introduces illustrative methods and supplies no independent duty-performance test. The original uncertainty remains.
The heading identifies a passkey example, not a mandatory exclusive method or evidence of performance.
The cross-device passkey example assumes an already registered account passkey. That prerequisite and the permissive modality remain unrepresented.
Cross-device passkey login spans platform types and continues in unit 217. It is an example procedure, not an answer to either original question.
The example permits login using an unbound device before offering binding. Login and binding must remain separate events.
Binding follows the client's choice in this example. The text does not impose automatic or universal binding after passkey login.
This outcome fragment depends on the registered passkey, login and client choice in preceding units. It cannot establish a standalone duty state.
This heading introduces biometric verification against internal records as another example. It supplies no quantitative acceptance criteria.
Biometric collection during account opening is a prerequisite within Example 2. It must not be generalized into a requirement for every authentication alternative.
Example 2 specifies facial data collection and verification, completed by liveness and storage conditions in following units. Performance is unknown.
Liveness detection and secure storage are substantive conditions in Example 2. Their adequacy cannot be replaced by an opaque compliance fact.
The Database definition links enrolment records to later verification across the page boundary. This dependency remains material and unresolved in the proposal.
The liveness footnote describes a selfie and prompted actions. It does not define a numerical performance threshold or establish successful verification.
Blinking and head-turning illustrate liveness prompts. These examples do not prove that a particular implementation resists spoofing.
Preventing deepfakes is the stated purpose of the liveness process, not a supplied performance measurement. Adequacy remains unresolved.
This address is page furniture, not a substantive authentication duty. It cannot resolve the synthetic second-duty, exception or edition concern.
The Chinese address is page furniture. Its presence supplies no legal connection to the original questions or resolution of edition uncertainty.
Contact information supplies no independent duty or evidence of performance. The synthetic concern remains retained.
The page number marks a continuation, not a substantive rule or proof of the applicable edition.
This continues Example 2 when a client seeks new-device binding, relying on biometric enrolment before the page break. It does not create a rebinding obligation for existing bound devices.
Initial application login is one step in the biometric example. It is not sufficient verification for binding by itself.
Username and password support the initial step; subsequent biometric and liveness checks remain required within the example. Credentials alone do not establish robustness.
The new-device application prompts a selfie, with liveness checks completed in unit 236. This operational step remains unrepresented.
Selfie capture and liveness checks are cumulative steps in Example 2. Their completion and adequacy are unknown.
The collected information must be verified against the specified reference records. A generic biometric-success fact would omit this dependency.
Verification uses the Database and is independent of device-native biometric functions. This distinction cannot be collapsed into local device unlocking.
This fragment completes the exclusion of reliance on device-native biometrics for the described database comparison. It does not answer second.duty.
The matching condition leads to binding within Example 2, subject to its preceding enrolment, login, liveness and comparison steps. Matching thresholds remain unspecified.
This binding outcome depends on the preceding conditional procedure. It cannot serve as an independent overall-compliance result.
The heading introduces personal identity document verification as an alternative example. It does not make that method universally mandatory.
Example 3 concerns a requested new-device binding, not compelled rebinding of existing devices. The original question mapping remains unsupported.
Login on the new device precedes document verification. Treating this initial step as sufficient would omit the remainder of Example 3.
Username and password are initial credentials in the document-verification example; authenticity, record matching and selfie comparison remain separate steps.
The application prompt begins document capture and must be read with units 247–248. It supplies no standalone performance predicate.
Identity-document images are required within Example 3; a Hong Kong identity card is an example, not the only document stated to be acceptable.
Multiple-angle capture serves document authenticity verification. The source supplies no measurable authenticity-performance threshold.
Extraction of the unique identity number is one step in a larger verification sequence. Extraction alone does not establish identity.
OCR extraction is followed by cross-checking against a specified prior record. Neither an OCR-success fact nor a gift result captures that dependency.
The reference identity record comes from account opening and is stored in the Database. Its provenance must remain part of the comparison.
This continuation specifies the reference record's storage location and depends on the earlier Database definition. It is not an independent duty.
Selfie comparison is an additional step in Example 3 and must not be omitted merely because document data match the Database.
The selfie is compared with the document photograph to address stolen-document use. No measured matching accuracy or guaranteed prevention is established.
The final document-data matching condition must be read with all preceding Example 3 steps, including authenticity and selfie checks. It does not establish overall compliance.
The binding outcome completes a conditional example. It neither proves actual performance nor resolves the unspecified second duty.
Physical verification is another illustrative route. Its availability must be retained alongside passkey and remote verification alternatives.
Example 4 concerns a client wishing to bind a new device. It does not displace the existing-bound-device exception.
An in-person office visit is a permitted identity-verification example, not a universal requirement. Its conditions continue across the partition boundary.
The physical-verification example generally requires valid identity documents matching internal records. The qualification and subsequent device requirement remain material.
Matching internal records and presenting the intended device belong to the same physical-verification procedure. Neither can be treated as an isolated complete test.

Additional supporting proof is conditional on appropriateness. This final qualification completes Example 4, not every source duty; the synthetic links from all units to this unit establish no legal dependency or resolution.

questions.rationale: Retained as an original question, but the supplied cybersecurity source does not support a distributor gift-prohibition decision. The synthetic reading proposes no legal interpretation and has no executable formalization. No Boolean answer is justified.

Retained separately. The duty is unidentified, and the performance question conflicts with its PROHIBITED classification and gift-based true/false meanings. The source contains multiple independent duties; none may silently be selected as the second duty. No performance determination is supported.

remaining_uncertainty: All 263 supplied units inform this assessment. Exactly the 65 selected concerns are disposed of here; other batches remain unchanged, and this response does not complete the whole-source reconciliation.

The original reading expressly disclaims a legal interpretation. Its Fund subject, inclusive-lower-boundary distinction and gift questions do not match the supplied authentication source. No replacement question or executable result is proposed.

The existing-client exception in unit 13 removes a requirement to rebind already bound devices; it does not remove login-security duties, new-device verification requirements or other account protections.

Unit 49 states implementation as soon as practicable and no later than 8 July 2027, with immediate implementation expected for large internet brokers. The supplied text does not define large internet brokers or reduce practicability and immediacy to exact measurable tests.

The applicable source edition and complete incorporated requirements remain unresolved. Five dependencies have null source hashes; document locators and span identifiers do not establish version currency or supply missing provisions.

Passkeys and bound devices are examples, with platform suitability and robust verification still requiring assessment. The source preserves other robust controls and physical verification alternatives; it does not establish a closed list of acceptable methods.

The OTP restriction must be read with transitional use, enhanced monitoring, immediate suspension or restriction for suspicious activity, and the differing passkey-setup scenarios during and after the implementation period.

Passkey certification, strong initial verification, authorization for additional passkeys, recovery and revocation controls, client guidance and synchronized-passkey safeguards remain separate requirements. A successful login or binding does not establish their satisfaction.

The general three-passkey/device limits preserve assessment before approving more; timeout expectations preserve justified longer periods with close monitoring. Neither exception is an unconditional exemption.

Client notifications, surveillance, incident containment, immediate reporting, root-cause analysis, remediation, client education, testing before deployment, rollout, implementation support, difficulty notification and management oversight remain distinct duties with their respective timing and qualifications.

Robustness, adequacy, liveness effectiveness, biometric and document matching criteria, and appropriateness of additional proof are not supplied as quantitative executable standards. No fact values or overall-compliance facts are inferred.

Appendix examples depend on preceding and following fragments across partition and page boundaries. Headings, addresses, contact details and page numbers do not become independent obligations merely because every unit is marked normative.
Coverage links to unit 262 and unit 0 are synthetic accounting links. Unit 262's conditional supporting-proof requirement neither governs every unit nor resolves the unspecified second duty.
